newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Serb war crimes suspect says has nothing to hide.
newsitem.headline: Serb war crimes suspect says has nothing to hide.

text.p: A Bosnian Serb charged with crimes against humanity during the Bosnian war in 1992 said on Tuesday he wanted to cooperate with the U.N. war crimes tribunal, where he has been on trial since May.

Dusan Tadic, cross-examined by prosecutors for the first time, said he had played no part in ethnic cleasing and wanted to clear his name. "I don't think I have got anything to hide," he told prosecution lawyer Alan Tieger.

Tadic, 41, a former reserve policeman and cafe owner, was giving his third day of testimony before the U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia after being called by the defence in a surprise move on Friday.
He is accused of helping to round up non-Serbs in northwest Bosnia and beating and killing them at the Serb-run detention camps of Omarska, Trnopolje and Keraterm.

Tieger asked him about his attitude towards the various religious groups living in the area at the time. "You have spoken of the good people of Kozarac. But those Moslems are not there any more," Tieger said.
"They have been driven from their homes. Many were rounded up by Serb forces and put into camps."
Tadic, who remained calm throughout the cross-examination and gave his answers through an interpreter: replied: "I did not take part in such activities. I do not know what happened to them."
Tieger also accused Tadic of organising a plebiscite in November 1991 for Serbs in the municipality of Prijedor on behalf of the Serbian Democratic Party.
He said Tadic denounced Serbs who did not vote and informed Serb authorities about others who were married to either Moslems or Croats.
Tadic denied he had publicly denounced non-voters and said he simply thought that people who did not take part in public affairs could not be trusted.
Tieger asked Tadic if he had seen busloads of Moslem prisoners being transported from a village near Prijedor to camps at Omarska and Keraterm in July 1992.
"Maybe I saw a couple of buses but I don't know where they came from or where they were going," Tadic said.
Tadic has maintained his innocence throughout the case, claiming he is a victim of mistaken identity.

The tribunal has indicted 75 suspected war criminials but has only seven in its custody. The rest, including former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadic and his military commander Radko Mladic, remain free.
